name: Crispy Double-Fried Chicken Tenders
desc: Salt-brined tenders pressed into starch, dipped in sparkling-water batter and fried twice.

source.title: Perfect Chicken Tender (test results)
source.evidence: Saved Instagram reel; caption and on-screen text captured in the owner's saved-recipes export

ingredients.raw: 1/2 cup dill pickle juice (optional, for flavor)
1/2 cup cold sparkling water (club soda or seltzer)
4 to 6 cups vegetable or canola oil (about 1 1/2 inches deep)

steps: Brine: stir the salt (and pickle juice, if using) into the cold water until dissolved. Add the chicken and refrigerate 20 minutes.
Whisk the batter's cornstarch, flour, baking powder and salt in a bowl and refrigerate it dry until you're ready to fry.

Take the chicken out of the brine and pat it dry. Stir the dry-mix cornstarch and flour together. Coat each tender in it, pressing it firmly into the meat. Set on a rack and let rest while the oil heats.
Heat the oil in a heavy pot to 320°F.
Whisk the sparkling water into the dry batter mix just until combined; small lumps are fine. Dip each coated tender in the batter and let the excess drip off.
First fry: fry in batches, without crowding, about 3 minutes until very pale golden. Drain on a rack and rest 10 to 20 minutes.
Second fry: heat the oil to 390°F and fry the tenders again 2 to 3 minutes until deep golden and crisp, and the thickest one reads 165°F inside. Drain on a rack and serve hot.
tips: Every brine the creator tested, except plain water, tenderized about the same. A 20-minute salt brine did as well as an overnight buttermilk one.
Pickle juice was the only brine that changed the flavor.
Starchy coatings came out crispier than the others and kept the oil cleaner.
Battered tenders had a much better crust than dry-dredged ones, and sparkling water made the best batter. A single or double dip made little difference.
Pressing the coating in and letting it rest was the biggest factor in a craggy crust. Double frying helped a little.
Use club soda or seltzer; sparkling mineral water has fewer bubbles.
The creator calls the dry mix only "starch-heavy"; the 3:1 cornstarch to flour split here is an estimate.
